title: Summer Sports League
theme: A Class 6 student named Avi starts a summer sports league in their housing colony. Make decisions to grow it into something amazing!
description: Build and manage a summer sports league in your housing colony. Navigate financial challenges, rivalry, community dynamics, and learn what it takes to be a young entrepreneur.
subject: Entrepreneurship
cultural_context: Indian housing colony, summer vacation setting
how_to_play: You are {name}, a {class} student starting a summer sports league in your housing colony.
Each round (week) presents a real entrepreneurship challenge with 4 choices.
Watch your League Status dashboard — players, money, reputation, and expenses are all connected.
Random events like rain, festivals, and equipment damage will test your resilience.
NPCs (Vikram, Rohit, Sharma Uncle, Meghna, Parents) react to your decisions.
Hidden metrics track your entrepreneurial thinking, balance, adaptability, vision, and ethics.
Aim for balanced growth — maximizing one metric at the expense of others will backfire!
learning_objectives: Understand basic entrepreneurship concepts: pricing, revenue, expenses, profit
Practice making decisions with trade-offs and incomplete information
Develop strategic thinking about resource allocation and growth
Learn to handle competition, crises, and community dynamics
Build empathy for diverse stakeholder perspectives
Understand the difference between short-term gains and long-term sustainability

glossary_terms.definition: The total money coming into your business. For Avi's league, revenue comes from player fees and special events. Revenue is NOT the same as profit — you still have to subtract expenses.
The money going OUT of your business to keep it running. Equipment, water, renting space — these are all expenses. Lower expenses mean more profit, but cutting too much can hurt quality.
What's left after you subtract expenses from revenue. Profit = Revenue - Expenses. A business needs positive profit to survive long-term.
How you decide what to charge. Price too high and you lose customers. Price too low and you can't cover costs. The best price balances affordability with sustainability.
Dividing your customers into groups based on their needs. Like having a Junior and Senior division — same league, but tailored experiences for different groups.
When someone else offers a similar product or service. Rohit starting his own league is competition. It pushes you to be better, but it can also squeeze your margins.
The unique reason someone should choose YOUR league over alternatives. It's not just about price — it's about the total experience: coaching, community, fun, learning.
Giving tasks to others instead of doing everything yourself. Great leaders delegate so they can focus on the big picture. Hiring Priya as assistant coach is delegation.
Can your business keep running for a long time? A sustainable business covers its costs, keeps customers happy, and doesn't burn out its founder.
How much value you get back from money you spend. If you spend Rs.900 on equipment and it helps you keep 5 more players (Rs.200/week each), that's a great ROI.
Raising money from a group of people, each contributing a small amount. Asking parents to chip in for equipment is a form of crowdfunding.
Changing your business direction when circumstances change. Moving from outdoor to indoor games during monsoon is a pivot. The best entrepreneurs pivot fast.

A business model where someone creates a system that others can copy and run in different locations. Writing 'The League Playbook' so other colonies can start their own league is creating a franchise model.
Anyone who is affected by or has an interest in your business. Players, parents, neighbors, Sharma Uncle — they're all stakeholders in Avi's league.
Something that protects your business from competition, like a castle moat. Unique features that competitors can't easily copy — like coaching certificates or a parent WhatsApp group — are your moat.

endings.title: Colony Legend
endings.message: You did it! You built something incredible from nothing — just a kid with Rs.200 and a dream. Your summer sports league became the talk of the entire colony. Parents trust you, kids adore you, and even Rohit secretly admires what you built. Sharma Uncle tells everyone about 'that brilliant Class 6 entrepreneur.' You didn't just run a league — you proved that age is just a number when it comes to leadership. Colony Legend status: UNLOCKED.

endings.title: League Champion
endings.message: A strong showing! Your league had its ups and downs, but you kept it running all summer. Players had fun, parents were mostly happy, and you learned more about business in 12 weeks than most adults learn in years. You made tough calls, handled crises, and came out stronger. League Champion — well earned!

endings.title: Solid Organizer
endings.message: Not bad at all! Your league was a decent operation — some weeks were great, some were tough. You kept things going even when it got hard. The experience taught you valuable lessons about money, people, and leadership. With what you know now, next summer could be legendary.

endings.title: Learning Experience
endings.message: Your league struggled, but every failure teaches something valuable. Maybe the pricing was off, or a crisis hit too hard, or you made a few wrong calls. That's okay! The greatest entrepreneurs in history failed multiple times before succeeding. The fact that you TRIED puts you ahead of everyone who didn't.

endings.title: Back to the Drawing Board
endings.message: The league didn't survive the summer. Maybe the money ran out, or players left, or the crises were too much. But here's the secret: EVERY great entrepreneur has a story of their first failure. This isn't the end — it's the beginning of your learning journey. Come back, try different strategies, and build something amazing. The playground is waiting.

endings.title: The Mentor
endings.message: You sit under the banyan tree where it all began. Two younger kids, Kabir and Neha, are huddled next to you, notebook open, taking furious notes. You walk them through the schedule, the payment system, the team rotation — everything. When you hand over the scorebook, Kabir holds it like it's a cricket trophy. Next summer, this won't be your league. It'll be theirs. And the summer after that, someone else's. You're not just leaving a league behind. You're leaving a pattern. Legacy isn't what you keep. It's what keeps going without you.

endings.title: The Author
endings.message: The Summer Sports League Manual, printed in crisp blue ink, sits in your hands. Fifty pages. Every mistake you made, every system you built, every NPC you navigated — documented. You've already emailed it to three parent WhatsApp groups in nearby colonies. One mother from Greater Noida messaged back within an hour: 'We're starting this next week.' The most satisfying thing about leadership isn't being the hero of one story. It's writing the playbook so a hundred heroes can rise. You didn't just build a league. You built a template. That's scale.

endings.title: The Loyalist
endings.message: Weekends are yours now. Saturday mornings, the compound fills up. You've cut the league down — shorter sessions, fewer kids, lower intensity — but it's still alive. Your math teacher notices you're tired. Your cousin says you're 'obsessed.' But every Saturday, Arjun asks when the next tournament is, and that's all you need. The league is smaller. Your ownership is total. This is the quieter choice — the one where you don't let go. Not everything has to scale. Some things just have to survive.

endings.title: The Celebration
endings.message: The final tournament runs on a perfect cloudless Sunday. Three sports, four hours, twenty-five players, sixty parents watching. You hand out medals you spent Rs.100 making. Gupta uncle — yes, Gupta uncle — shakes your hand at the end: 'Well done, beta. Ananya wouldn't stop talking about you at dinner.' When the banyan tree casts its long evening shadow over an empty compound, you feel something strange: peace. You didn't drag the league into the school year where it would've slowly faded. You ended it on its highest note. Sometimes the best founders are the ones who know when to close beautifully.

rounds.title: The Big Idea
rounds.situation:
It's Day 10 of summer vacation. You're lying on the sofa watching your ceiling fan spin, the TV remote long lost behind the cushions. Through the window you can see Arjun and his sister sitting on the compound wall, doing absolutely nothing. Down the lane, three kids are throwing stones at a mango tree because there's literally nothing else to do.

That's when the idea hits you. What if you organized a proper sports league? Not just random games, but a real league with teams, scores, rotations between cricket, football, and badminton, and a winner certificate every Friday. You could charge Rs.50 per week per kid. With 35 kids in the colony, that's potentially Rs.1,750 a week if everyone joins.

But wait. You've never done anything like this before. Do kids even want a structured league? Will parents pay? Your friend Meera says, "Just start and see what happens." Your older cousin says, "Do some research first, you'll waste time otherwise."
rounds.goal: Decide how to launch your summer sports league
rounds.coaching_moment: Market validation means asking one simple question BEFORE you start: does anyone actually want what I'm about to build?

rounds.title: What's the Right Price?
rounds.situation:
Week 1 of the league is done. You've got players showing up and the energy is real. But now the money question hits hard. You set Rs.50 per week as the entry fee, but reactions are mixed.

Rohan's mom stopped you at the gate this morning: "Rs.50 every week? That's Rs.200 a month! My son can play for free in the park." Meanwhile, Arjun's dad actually said, "Only Rs.50? For a proper organized league with certificates? That's very reasonable, beta."

Three kids dropped out after Week 1 saying it's too expensive. But two NEW kids from the adjacent lane want to join because they heard it's 'a real league, not just random play.'

You sit under the banyan tree, calculator in hand, weighing your options. Your costs are real: shuttlecocks (Rs.60/week), a proper football (Rs.150 one-time), and certificates (Rs.5 each). Price too low, you can't sustain this. Too high, and half the colony walks.
rounds.coaching_moment: Pricing isn't just math — it's psychology. Your price is your first advertisement.

rounds.title: Getting Equipped
rounds.situation:
The league is picking up steam. You've got a routine going: cricket on Monday-Wednesday, football on Thursday-Friday, badminton on Saturday. The problem? Your equipment is embarrassing.

The old cricket bat has a crack running down the handle, held together with electrical tape. The football you borrowed from Meera is so deflated it barely bounces. And you don't even OWN badminton rackets; you've been borrowing two mismatched ones from Auntie next door (who wants them back for her Pune trip next week).

Rakesh, the local sports shop owner on Main Road, knows you've been running the league. He pulls you aside: "Beta, I can give you a starter kit: 2 cricket bats, a real football, 4 badminton rackets, shuttlecocks (50-pack), and a bag of tennis balls. Full price is Rs.400. For you? Rs.250. But I need cash upfront."

You check your wallet and your collection tin. Rs.250 is a lot when you count every rupee you've earned. Every rupee counts.
rounds.goal: Decide how to equip the league within your budget
rounds.coaching_moment: Resource management asks: what do I NEED vs. what do I WANT vs. what can I WAIT for? The best entrepreneurs separate these ruthlessly.

rounds.title: Not Everyone's Happy
rounds.situation:
Three weeks into the league, and you have a problem you didn't see coming. It's not about money or equipment. It's about PEOPLE.

The 8-9 year olds are getting completely outplayed in cricket by the 13-14 year olds. Little Ananya came home crying after Vikram's fast bowling scared her and she got hit on the pad. Her father, Gupta uncle, is very upset: "This is dangerous! My daughter is NOT coming back unless you fix this."

Meanwhile, the older kids are bored. Vikram tells you point-blank: "Bhai, playing with babies is boring. Me and my friends want a REAL challenge. If you don't make it competitive, we'll go play at the municipal ground instead."

Your current 22 players are split: roughly 10 younger kids (8-10), 8 middle (11-12), and 4 older (13-14). The older kids are your best players AND your biggest spenders. The younger kids are the majority. You can't afford to lose either group.
rounds.goal: Resolve the age and skill gap without losing your community
rounds.coaching_moment: Customer segmentation means your players are not all the same. The 8-year-old playing for fun and the 14-year-old playing to win need different experiences.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: An Indian housing colony cricket ground, a small girl (age 9) crying while older boys celebrate, mixed emotions, a young organizer looking concerned, cartoon Pixar style, afternoon light, emotional scene
rounds.reflection_prompt: Think about a time when you saw someone being left out because they weren't as skilled. How did it make you feel? What could have been done differently?

choices.feedback: Ananya is back! The juniors have their own matches now. It costs more to run two divisions, but both groups are thriving. Fair play wins.

rounds.title: The Money Squeeze
rounds.situation:
It's Week 4. You open your collection tin and your stomach drops. After equipment purchases, shuttlecock replacements, certificate printing, and the football pump you had to buy when the old one broke, your cash is dangerously low.

You do the math on the back of a notebook. Weekly income from players: variable (some paid late, two haven't paid at all). Weekly expenses: Rs.25 for shuttlecocks, Rs.5 for certificates, Rs.10 for miscellaneous. That's Rs.40/week going OUT. If even three kids skip payment, you're in the red.

To make matters worse, the monsoon season is approaching. You need to buy a tarpaulin (Rs.150) to cover the badminton court area, or rain will wipe out two of your weekly sessions. That's money you absolutely don't have.

You feel the first real pang of regret. Maybe you should have just watched TV all summer like everyone else.

rounds.title: The Rival League
rounds.situation:
The blow comes on a Tuesday morning. You're setting up the cricket pitch when Meera runs up, out of breath: "Rohit from B-Block is starting his own sports league. He's charging only Rs.30. And his dad bought him brand-new equipment."

Your heart sinks. Rohit is popular, his family has money, and B-Block has another 20 kids who were never part of your colony league. But now he's openly poaching YOUR players. Three of your regulars already told you they're 'going to check out Rohit's league' this weekend.

You cycle past B-Block that evening. Rohit has a proper setup: new stumps, colored bibs for teams, and a giant whiteboard with a bracket system. His dad is standing there, arms crossed, looking proud. Rohit waves at you with a smirk.

This is the first time your league's existence is threatened not by internal problems, but by external competition. What do you do?

rounds.title: Growing Pains
rounds.situation:
The league survived Rohit's challenge and is actually growing. You now have 28 players across two blocks. Parents are talking about it at morning walks. Sharma uncle from the society committee said, "Beta, well done. Maybe we can make this an official society activity."

But you're drowning. You wake up at 7 AM to set up the pitch. You manage teams from 8-10 AM. You collect money during lunch. You update the scoreboard in the evening. You print certificates at night. You haven't done ANYTHING fun this vacation. Your mom said last night: "You look more stressed than your father going to office."

Three things need your attention simultaneously: (1) New kids from C-Block want to join but you physically can't manage more players alone. (2) The scoreboard system is a mess, with hand-written scores getting smudged and lost. (3) Two parents complained that last week's teams were unfair.

You realize the truth: the league has outgrown YOU. You are the bottleneck.

rounds.title: The Tough Day
rounds.situation:
This is the worst day of your summer. Everything that could go wrong, did.

It started during the cricket match. Vikram accused Arjun of cheating: 'He nicked the ball! That's out!' Arjun shouted back: 'I didn't touch it! You're lying!' Within seconds, eight kids were arguing. Vikram pushed Arjun. Arjun stumbled and hurt his elbow. He started tearing up. Parents appeared on their balconies.

Then Gupta uncle stormed down: 'I KNEW this would happen! This league is a MESS. I'm pulling my daughter AND telling other parents.' Three parents gathered at the gate, arms crossed. They want answers.

Meanwhile, you just discovered that Rs.60 has gone missing from the collection tin. You had asked Rohan (one of your assistants) to collect this week's fees. He swears he collected everything. But the math doesn't add up.

You're standing in the compound with a hurt kid, angry parents, a missing-money mystery, and a league on the verge of falling apart. EVERY OPTION IS PAINFUL. There is no clean exit.
rounds.coaching_moment: Crisis leadership: acknowledge, show you care, demonstrate a plan. Stop further harm first, then stabilize, investigate, rebuild.

rounds.reflection_prompt: Have you ever been blamed for something you didn't do, or seen someone else get blamed unfairly? How did it feel? What's the right way to handle accusations?

choices.feedback: The parents listen. Some are still angry. But your honesty earns respect. You promise safety changes and a new secure collection system. Most parents decide to give you another chance — even though Vikram-Arjun and the missing money are still unresolved.

rounds.title: Noise Complaint!
rounds.situation:
Just when you thought the worst was over, a notice appears on the colony notice board. Hand-written in red pen by Sharma uncle, the Society President:

"NOTICE: Multiple residents have complained about excessive noise from the children's sports activities between 8-10 AM. This is disturbing senior citizens and work-from-home residents. The Management Committee will discuss whether to BAN outdoor sports activities during morning hours at the next meeting (this Sunday). Residents are invited to attend."

Your league plays from 8 to 10 AM. If the committee bans morning play, your league is effectively finished.

You have five days before Sunday's meeting. The watchman Raju kaka tells you quietly: 'Beta, Mrs. Kapoor from third floor and Mr. Joshi from ground floor are the main complainers. Everyone else doesn't care much.'
rounds.goal: Keep the league alive despite regulatory pressure
rounds.coaching_moment: Stakeholders aren't just customers. Listen, understand, adapt — that's how you survive the rules around you.

rounds.title: Monsoon Mayhem
rounds.situation:
The monsoon hits with a vengeance. For three straight days, rain hammers the compound so hard you can't even see across the courtyard. The cricket pitch is a lake. The badminton court is a waterfall. Your WhatsApp group is filled with sad emojis and 'when will it stop?' messages.

Day 4, the rain pauses but the ground is a mud pit. Day 5, it rains again. The forecast shows intermittent heavy rain for the next two weeks. Your outdoor league is effectively paralyzed.

This is not a problem you can solve by working harder or spending money. The FUNDAMENTAL assumption of your business (outdoor play) has been undermined by something completely outside your control. You need to either innovate or watch your league slowly fade.

Your players are getting restless. Two have already said they're 'done for the summer.' You have one week before the league becomes irrelevant.

rounds.title: The Big Offer
rounds.situation:
You get an unexpected phone call. It's Meghna Auntie, who runs the 'Little Champions Academy,' a proper coaching institute for kids in your area. She's seen your league and she's impressed.

"Beta, I have a proposal. Your league has something my academy doesn't: community, fun, and real engagement. My academy has what you don't: professional coaches, indoor facilities, and a brand that parents trust. Let's partner. I'll bring my coaches to your league twice a week, provide indoor space during monsoon, and add your league to my marketing. In return, I want 40% of all revenue and the right to use 'Little Champions x [Your League Name]' branding."

She adds: "Also, I'm willing to pay you Rs.2,000 upfront as a signing bonus. And if this works, I want to do this every year as a formal program. You'd be the 'Community Engagement Director.' That's a real title on your school applications."

This is the biggest opportunity of the summer. But also the most complex decision.

rounds.title: Legacy
rounds.situation:
It's the last week of summer vacation. School starts Monday. The monsoon has softened into occasional drizzles. The compound, which was a deserted, boring wasteland eight weeks ago, has been transformed by YOUR league.

You stand at the banyan tree where you first had the idea. The scoreboard you built hangs from the wall. Twenty-five kids are warming up for today's session. Parents are sitting on the boundary, chatting, some cheering. Even Mrs. Kapoor waved at you from her balcony this morning.

But reality is setting in. School means homework, tuitions, early mornings. You can't run the league anymore. Or can you? The question isn't whether the league was successful (it was). The question is: what happens to it when you're gone?

Raju kaka walks up: 'Beta, the kids are asking if the league will run on weekends during school. And three parents asked if you can do this again next summer.' You smile. But the smile hides a bigger question: what do you want your legacy to be?
rounds.goal: Decide the final fate of your league
rounds.coaching_moment: The ultimate test of what you built is: can it survive without you? If yes, you built something real.

choices.feedback: You spend the last week training Ananya and Sahil. They're nervous but excited. When you hand over the equipment box, Ananya says 'I'll make you proud.' You've created something bigger than yourself.
